abstracts.title: Zhili Chen
abstracts.description:
Violence has long been a central component of game design, yet it is often treated primarily
as a mechanic of challenge or spectacle rather than as a meaningful expressive tool. This
project investigates violence as a form of expression in games, asking how violent systems
can convey emotion, character, and narrative rather than merely serve as interactive conflict
resolution.
This research contributes to ongoing discourse by reframing violence not as content alone,
but as a designed language embedded within player interaction. Drawing from analyses of
existing games, film theory, and interactive media studies, the project examines how timing,
player agency, repetition, and feedback systems shape the emotional and narrative meaning
of violent acts. Particular attention is given to how systems of escalation, loss of control, and
embodiment can transform violence into a vehicle for expressing psychological states.
The practical component of this research is a prototype game that situates combat within the
everyday life of a troubled high school student. In this work, fighting is not the primary goal
but one aspect of a broader simulation, where player actions accumulate toward moments of
loss of control, represented through a “possession” system. This design explores how violence
can emerge from systemic pressure rather than player intention alone.
The findings suggest that when integrated with narrative systems and player state, violence
can function as a powerful expressive medium, capable of communicating internal conflict
and social tension. This project demonstrates how recontextualizing violence can expand its
role within game design beyond spectacle toward meaningful expression.
